subtopics.name: Integer arithmetic, overflow & floor/ceil
subtopics.summary: The everyday arithmetic every Div 2/3/4 A-B problem relies on: integer division, remainders, ceiling division, parity and 64-bit overflow. Recognise it when a statement asks for a count or minimum that can be written as a closed formula of the inputs.
learn: Use long long whenever a product or sum can exceed about 2*10^9; cast before multiplying (1LL*a*b).
Ceiling division for positives: (a+b-1)/b; in C++ '/' truncates toward zero and % can be negative for negative operands.
Parity reasoning: the sum of k odd numbers has the parity of k; many A problems reduce to an even/odd check.
Count multiples of k in [l,r] as r/k-(l-1)/k; the k-th number not divisible by n is a closed formula.
Avoid floating point for exact integer answers: compute integer sqrt with a correction loop, compare a*d vs c*b instead of a/b vs c/d.
Derive a formula on small cases by hand, then double-check edge cases (0, 1, equal values, maximum constraints).

subtopics.name: Sums, series & closed formulas
subtopics.summary: Arithmetic and geometric series, sum of squares, and the habit of turning a loop over a huge range into an O(1) formula. Appears whenever n is up to 10^9-10^18 and the answer is a sum of a regular pattern.
learn: 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2; sum of the first k odd numbers is k^2; sum of squares n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
Geometric series a(r^k-1)/(r-1); sum of powers of two 2^0+...+2^(k-1)=2^k-1.
Minimum/maximum sums of k distinct numbers from [1..n] are prefix/suffix arithmetic series, and every value in between is reachable.
Combine a monotone closed-form sum with binary search when you need the first k reaching a target.
Compute range sums of arithmetic sequences as (first+last)*count/2 and beware overflow of the intermediate product.
Telescoping and pairing tricks (Gauss pairing) simplify many 'sum over a pattern' tasks.

subtopics.name: Digits & number bases
subtopics.summary: Manipulating decimal digits and representations in base k (including binary): digit sums, round numbers, repunits, counting how digits change. Recognise it when a property is stated in terms of the decimal/binary representation of a number.
learn: Extract digits with n%10 and n/=10; the number of digits of n is floor(log10 n)+1 but compute it with integer loops.
A number written in base k with digits 0/1 corresponds to a subset of powers of k (bitmask of the index).
Repunits 11...1 and 'numbers of identical digits' can be enumerated directly (only 9*18 such numbers below 10^18).
Large numbers of 11, 111, ... can be reduced: any representation only needs 11 and 111 (since 1111 = 11*101).
Count digit changes when incrementing from l to r by summing r/10^i - l/10^i over i.
Divisibility rules: by 3/9 via digit sum, by 2/5/10 via last digit, by 4/25 via last two digits.

subtopics.name: Divisibility & divisors in O(√n)
subtopics.summary: Divisors come in pairs (d, n/d), so all divisors of n can be enumerated in O(√n). This is the first tool for problems like 'find the smallest/largest divisor', 'split n into factors' or 'minimum packages of equal size'.
learn: Loop d from 1 while d*d<=n; if n%d==0 record d and n/d (avoid recording the square root twice).
The smallest divisor >1 of n is prime; the largest proper divisor is n / smallest prime factor.
A number has an odd divisor >1 iff it is not a power of two.
The number of divisors of n<=10^9 is at most 1344, of n<=10^18 at most 103680, so iterating over divisors is usually cheap.
To check divisibility of a product without overflow, reduce factors with gcd first.
Reconstruct n from its full divisor list: n = smallest * largest, then verify the list.

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Number of divisors / sum of divisors

problems.name: Omkar and Last Class of Math

subtopics.name: GCD, LCM & Euclid's algorithm
subtopics.summary: gcd(a,b) via Euclid runs in O(log min(a,b)); lcm(a,b)=a/gcd(a,b)*b. Key identities like gcd(a,b)=gcd(a,b-a) and 'the gcd of a prefix changes at most log times' unlock many Div 2 B-D problems.
learn: Euclid: gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a mod b); std::gcd / std::lcm in C++17; compute lcm as a/gcd*b to avoid overflow.
gcd(a+x, b+x) = gcd(a+x, b-a): differences turn 'gcd of shifted array' into a fixed gcd of differences.
gcd(a1..an) can only decrease, and each decrease divides it by at least 2, so prefix gcds take O(log) distinct values.
Reduce ratios a:b by dividing by gcd to use them as hashable keys.
lcm grows fast: when lcm of a set exceeds a bound you can stop early.
gcd(a,b)=1 problems: consecutive integers are coprime; gcd(n, n+1)=1, gcd(n, 2n+1)=1.
Sparse table / segment tree over gcd answers range-gcd queries (gcd is idempotent).

resources.title: CPH: Primes and factors: Euclid's algorithm

subtopics.name: Primes, primality & Sieve of Eratosthenes
subtopics.summary: Trial division tests primality in O(√n); the Sieve of Eratosthenes marks all primes up to N in O(N log log N) and the linear sieve also produces smallest prime factors. Recognise it when many numbers up to 10^6-10^7 need prime information.
learn: Sieve: for each prime p, mark multiples starting at p*p; memory as vector<bool> or bitset for N=10^7.
Linear sieve computes spf[i] (smallest prime factor) and multiplicative functions in O(N).
Prime gaps are small (<~300 below 10^9) so 'next prime >= x' is a short trial-division loop.
Every even number >2 is not prime; Goldbach-style facts (every even number is a sum of two primes in contest ranges) appear in constructive tasks.
Deterministic Miller-Rabin with fixed bases tests 64-bit primality in O(log n) multiplications.
Segmented sieve finds primes in a range [L,R] with R up to 10^12 and R-L up to 10^6.

resources.title: CPH: Primes and factors: sieve of Eratosthenes

subtopics.name: Prime factorization & smallest-prime-factor sieve
subtopics.summary: Write n = p1^e1 ... pk^ek by trial division (O(√n)) or in O(log n) per query using a precomputed smallest-prime-factor array. Exponent vectors turn products, perfect powers, squares and divisibility questions into simple per-prime arithmetic.
learn: Trial division up to √n; whatever remains >1 is a prime factor.
With spf[] from a sieve, factorize any x<=N in O(log x) by repeated division.
a divides b iff every prime exponent of a is <= that of b; gcd/lcm take min/max exponents.
Perfect k-th power iff all exponents are divisible by k; reduce exponents mod k to get a canonical 'signature' (square-free part for k=2).
Legendre's formula: the exponent of p in n! is sum floor(n/p^i); trailing zeros of n! in base b use the limiting prime of b.
A number <=10^18 has at most 15 distinct prime factors; <=10^9 at most 9.

subtopics.name: Modular arithmetic
subtopics.summary: Doing all arithmetic modulo m (usually 10^9+7 or 998244353) to keep numbers small, and reasoning about remainders (pairs whose sum is divisible by k, cycles of last digits). Recognise 'print the answer modulo ...' or conditions on divisibility of sums.
learn: (a+b) mod m, (a-b+m) mod m, (a*b) mod m with 64-bit intermediates; never divide directly under a modulus.
Normalise negatives: ((x % m) + m) % m.
Group numbers by remainder: a+b divisible by k iff r_a + r_b ≡ 0 (mod k); count pairs with a map of remainders.
Pigeonhole: among m+1 numbers two share a remainder mod m, so if n>m the product of differences mod m is 0.
Last digits / remainders under repeated operations become periodic quickly; simulate until the cycle.
Algebraic tricks: multiply both sides by a factor to separate i and j (e.g. (a+b)(a^2+b^2) = (a^4-b^4)/(a-b)).

subtopics.name: Binary (fast) exponentiation
subtopics.summary: Compute a^b mod m in O(log b) by repeated squaring. Needed for counting answers like 2^n or (2^m-1)^n, for modular inverses via Fermat, and as the core of matrix exponentiation.
learn: Iterative pow: while(b){ if(b&1) r=r*a%m; a=a*a%m; b>>=1; }.
Reduce the base first (a%=m) and use 64-bit (or __int128 when m is ~10^18).
Counting independent binary choices gives powers of 2; choices per item with 'not all empty' give (2^m-1)^n.
The same doubling idea works for any associative operation (matrix multiply, function composition, binary lifting).
Exponent towers need Euler's theorem to reduce the exponent (see Euler phi).
Precompute powers in an array when you need many consecutive powers.

problems.name: Alice and the List of Presents

subtopics.name: Modular inverse & division mod p
subtopics.summary: x^{-1} mod p exists when gcd(x,p)=1; for prime p it equals x^{p-2} (Fermat). This is how fractions, expected values and binomial coefficients are output 'modulo 998244353'.
learn: For prime p: inv(x)=pow(x,p-2,p); for general m use extended Euclid (requires gcd(x,m)=1).
A fraction P/Q is printed as P*Q^{-1} mod p; add/multiply fractions directly in modular form.
Inverses of 1..n in O(n): inv[i] = -(p/i) * inv[p%i] mod p.
Inverse factorials: invfact[n]=pow(fact[n],p-2), then invfact[i-1]=invfact[i]*i.
Never take the inverse of a value that may be ≡0 mod p (e.g. n>=p in n!).
Division by 2 mod p is multiplication by (p+1)/2.

subtopics.name: Harmonic loops over multiples (n/1+n/2+...)
subtopics.summary: Iterating, for every d, over all multiples of d costs n/1+n/2+...+n/n = O(n log n). It powers 'for every value, look at its multiples/divisors' DP and gcd counting on value-indexed arrays.
learn: for(d=1;d<=n;d++) for(m=d;m<=n;m+=d) ... runs in O(n log n); use it to build divisor lists for all numbers up to n.
Count, for each g, how many array values are multiples of g using a frequency array (cnt[g] = sum of freq of multiples).
Longest chain where each element divides the next: dp over values pushing to multiples.
'Is g achievable as a gcd of a subset?' check gcd of all present multiples of g equals g.
Combine with going from large g to small to subtract over-counting (preparation for Möbius).
Minimum lcm pair: for each g, take the two smallest present multiples of g.

resources.title: CPH: Primes and factors (sum of divisors, harmonic bounds)

subtopics.name: Divisor functions & multiplicative functions
subtopics.summary: From n = ∏ p^e you get τ(n)=∏(e+1), σ(n)=∏(p^{e+1}-1)/(p-1) and the product of divisors. Multiplicative functions (f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for coprime a,b) can be sieved for all n<=N.
learn: Number of divisors τ(n)=∏(e_i+1); sum of divisors σ(n)=∏(1+p+...+p^e).
Product of divisors = n^{τ(n)/2}; reduce the exponent mod p-1 when working modulo a prime p.
Multiplicative functions (τ, σ, φ, μ, ω-related) can be computed for all n<=N by the linear sieve.
Count distinct prime factors ω(n) for all n with a sieve; 2^{ω(n)} counts coprime ordered factor pairs.
Sum of τ(i) or σ(i) over i<=N via sum over d of floor(N/d) (and d*floor(N/d)).
DP over divisors of values (dp[d] over multiples) for maximizing sums of prefix gcds.

resources.title: USACO Guide: Prefix Sums of Number-Theoretic Functions (Part 1)
CPH: Primes and factors: number and sum of factors
cp-algorithms: Number of divisors / sum of divisors

subtopics.name: Euler's totient, Fermat & Euler's theorem
subtopics.summary: φ(n) counts 1<=k<=n with gcd(k,n)=1, computed from the factorization as n∏(1-1/p). Euler's theorem a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) (Fermat for primes) lets you reduce huge exponents and explains periodicity of powers.
learn: φ(n)=n∏(1-1/p) over distinct primes p|n; sieve φ for all n<=N in O(N log log N).
Number of k in [0,m) with gcd(a+k, m) = gcd(a,m) is φ(m/gcd(a,m)).
Fermat: a^{p-1} ≡ 1 mod p for prime p not dividing a, so exponents reduce mod p-1 (CSES Exponentiation II).
Generalised Euler: for e >= log2 m, a^e ≡ a^{(e mod φ(m)) + φ(m)} (mod m) even if gcd(a,m)≠1 (power towers).
Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n, a frequent identity for gcd sums: Σ_i gcd(i,n) = Σ_{d|n} d·φ(n/d).
Exponents of a recurrence of products (f_n = f_{n-1}f_{n-2}...) live modulo p-1 and are found with matrix power.

subtopics.name: Extended Euclid & linear Diophantine equations
subtopics.summary: Extended Euclid finds x,y with ax+by=gcd(a,b). It solves ax+by=c (solvable iff gcd|c), gives modular inverses modulo non-primes, and solves linear congruences ax ≡ b (mod m).
learn: Recursive ext_gcd returns g and (x,y); all solutions: x+k·b/g, y-k·a/g.
ax+by=c has integer solutions iff gcd(a,b) divides c; scale the base solution by c/g.
To find non-negative or minimal solutions, shift k so that x is in [0, b/g).
If x+y should be small with a,b positive, brute force over one variable up to the other coefficient (bounded by b/g).
Linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod m): divide by g=gcd(a,m) (needs g|b), then multiply by the inverse of a/g mod m/g.
Watch overflow: coefficients can reach ~10^18; use __int128 for products.
Frobenius / Chicken McNugget: for coprime a,b>0 every integer > ab-a-b is a non-negative combination of a and b; ab-a-b itself is not.

subtopics.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
subtopics.summary: A system x ≡ a_i (mod m_i) with pairwise coprime moduli has a unique solution modulo ∏m_i; with general moduli it is merged pairwise via extended Euclid. Appears with periodic events, interactive 'guess x' tasks and with knowing x mod several small numbers.
learn: Merge two congruences x≡a1 (mod m1), x≡a2 (mod m2): solvable iff a1≡a2 (mod gcd); new modulus lcm(m1,m2).
Knowing x mod m_i for all i determines x mod lcm(m_i); a modulus k is determined iff k | lcm(m_i).
Interactive: learn x modulo several small coprime numbers (e.g. via gcd queries) and combine.
Periodic coincidences of two cycles of lengths n and m repeat every lcm(n,m); count them per residue class with CRT.
Pigeonhole over small primes: if for prime p every residue class is used twice, no shift works (Koxia).
Garner's algorithm reconstructs big numbers from residues modulo several primes.

resources.title: USACO Guide: Extended Euclidean Algorithm (Chinese Remainder Theorem)
CPH: Solving equations: Chinese remainder theorem

subtopics.name: Floor-division blocks (O(√n) distinct quotients)
subtopics.summary: floor(n/i) takes only O(√n) distinct values, and all i with the same quotient form a contiguous block [l, n/(n/l)]. This turns sums like Σ f(floor(n/i)) or Σ n mod i into O(√n) loops.
learn: Iterate blocks: for(l=1;l<=n;l=r+1){ q=n/l; r=n/q; ... }.
n mod i = n - i·floor(n/i), so Σ n mod i is computed block by block with arithmetic series.
For a fixed quotient q, the i with floor(n/i)=q are in [n/(q+1)+1, n/q].
DP of the form dp[x] = Σ_z dp[floor(x/z)] is sped up by grouping equal quotients or by pushing contributions to multiples ranges.
Conditions like floor(a/b) = a mod b reduce to a = k(b+1) with k<b; count pairs with block sums.
Combine with Möbius prefix sums for Σ_{i<=n} Σ_{j<=m} [gcd(i,j)=1] (iterate blocks where both n/i and m/i are constant: r=min(n/(n/l), m/(m/l))).
Σ_{i<n} floor((a·i+b)/c) has an O(log) Euclid-like algorithm (floor_sum, as in AtCoder Library) for when even O(√n) is too slow.

resources.title: USACO Guide: Prefix Sums of Number-Theoretic Functions (Part 1)
CPH: Primes and factors (sum of factors over ranges)

subtopics.name: Möbius function & inversion (gcd counting)
subtopics.summary: μ(n) is 0 if n has a squared prime factor, otherwise (-1)^{#primes}. Σ_{d|n} μ(d) = [n=1] lets you count coprime pairs/subsets and pairs with gcd exactly g by inclusion–exclusion over divisors.
learn: [gcd = 1] = Σ_{d | gcd} μ(d): count coprime pairs as Σ_d μ(d)·C(cnt_d, 2).
Number of non-empty subsets with gcd 1: Σ_d μ(d)(2^{cnt_d}-1) where cnt_d = number of multiples of d.
'Exactly g' from 'divisible by g': f(g) = F(g) - Σ_{k>=2} f(kg), computed from large to small (a Möbius inversion without μ).
Sieve μ with the linear sieve; only square-free d matter.
Möbius inversion: if F(n) = Σ_{d|n} f(d) then f(n) = Σ_{d|n} μ(d) F(n/d).
Dirichlet convolution view: μ * 1 = ε, φ * 1 = id; combine with floor blocks for large n.
For n up to 10^10-10^11, prefix sums of μ or φ come from Dirichlet hyperbola / Du's sieve in about O(n^{2/3}) (advanced).

resources.title: USACO Guide: Prefix Sums of Number-Theoretic Functions (Dirichlet convolution)

subtopics.name: Primitive roots & discrete logarithm (BSGS)
subtopics.summary: A primitive root g mod p generates all non-zero residues, so multiplication becomes addition of exponents. Baby-step giant-step solves a^x ≡ b (mod m) in O(√m). Rare but appears in recurrences of products and 'k-th root mod p' tasks.
learn: Primitive root of prime p: test candidates g with g^{(p-1)/q} ≠ 1 for every prime q | p-1.
BSGS: write x = i·k - j with k≈√m, store a^j·b in a hash map, scan a^{ik}.
Taking logs base a primitive root converts x^k ≡ b into k·y ≡ log b (mod p-1), a linear congruence.
Multiplicative recurrences f_n = ∏ f_{n-i}^{c_i} become linear recurrences on exponents mod p-1 (matrix power).
Pollard's rho with Miller–Rabin factorizes 64-bit numbers in about O(n^{1/4}) when trial division is too slow.
Discrete root / Tonelli–Shanks for modular square roots are the same toolbox.

problems.name: Lunar New Year and a Recursive Sequence

subtopics.name: Counting principles (sum & product rules)
subtopics.summary: Rule of sum, rule of product, counting pairs with a frequency map, and complementary counting. Most early 'count the number of ...' problems need nothing more, but the counts must be organised to avoid O(n^2).
learn: Product rule: independent choices multiply; sum rule: disjoint cases add.
Count pairs i<j with equal key as Σ C(cnt,2) using a map; pairs with different keys as total minus equal.
Complementary counting: count the bad configurations and subtract from all.
Count substrings of allowed characters as Σ len·(len+1)/2 over maximal blocks.
Count unordered pairs from two groups as |A|·|B| minus conflicting pairs (inclusion–exclusion lite).
Arranging n people in circles: divide by rotations (n-1)!/... for circular arrangements.

subtopics.name: Binomial coefficients & factorials mod p
subtopics.summary: C(n,k) counts k-subsets. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials mod p in O(n) to answer each C(n,k) in O(1); use Pascal's triangle for small n or non-prime modulus. Lucas's theorem handles C(n,k) mod a small prime.
learn: Precompute fact[0..N], invfact[0..N] once; C(n,k)=fact[n]·invfact[k]·invfact[n-k], 0 if k<0 or k>n.
When n is huge but k is small, compute C(n,k) = n(n-1)...(n-k+1)/k! directly in O(k).
Pascal: C(n,k)=C(n-1,k-1)+C(n-1,k), O(n^2) table, works for any modulus.
Identities: Σ_k C(n,k)=2^n, hockey stick Σ_{i} C(i,k)=C(n+1,k+1), Vandermonde Σ C(a,i)C(b,k-i)=C(a+b,k).
Multinomial n!/(c1!c2!...) counts arrangements of a multiset (distinct strings from letters).
Fix the element in a special role (the median, the minimum) and choose the rest with binomials.
Lucas: C(n,k) mod p = ∏ C(n_i,k_i) over base-p digits; C(n,k) is odd iff k & n == k (Xor Pyramid).

subtopics.name: Stars and bars & distributions
subtopics.summary: The number of ways to write n as an ordered sum of k non-negative integers is C(n+k-1, k-1); with positive parts C(n-1,k-1). Also counts non-decreasing sequences and multisets.
learn: n identical balls into k distinct boxes: C(n+k-1,k-1); each box >=1: C(n-1,k-1).
Non-decreasing sequences of length m with values in [1,n] are multisets: C(n+m-1,m).
Lower bounds: subtract them first; upper bounds: use inclusion–exclusion over violated boxes.
Group indistinguishable objects (pairs of adjacent pawns) and place them among free cells: C(free+groups, groups).
Combine two monotone arrays into one longer monotone sequence to reduce to a single stars-and-bars count.
Generating-function view: coefficient of x^n in (1-x)^{-k}.

resources.title: CPH: Binomial coefficients: boxes and balls

problems.name: Sasha and the Wedding Binary Search Tree

subtopics.name: Contribution technique (sum over all pairs/subsets)
subtopics.summary: Instead of enumerating all subarrays, pairs, paths or subsets, compute how much each element (or edge, or bit) contributes to the total and sum those contributions. A core trick behind 'sum over all ...' problems.
learn: Element a[i] lies in i·(n-i+1) subarrays (1-indexed); weight it accordingly.
Sum of |x_i - x_j| over pairs: sort and add x_i·(2i-n-1).
Edge (u,v) of a tree lies on size·(n-size) paths.
Bitwise sums: handle each bit separately and count pairs/subarrays where the bit is set.
Sorted-order arguments: after sorting, each element's role (max/min/median) is determined by its position.
Sum over all 2^n subsets: an element appears in 2^{n-1} of them.

subtopics.name: Inclusion–exclusion principle
subtopics.summary: |A1∪...∪An| = Σ|Ai| - Σ|Ai∩Aj| + ... . Used to count objects avoiding all 'bad' properties: integers coprime to a set of primes, permutations with no bad positions, grids with constraints in every row/column.
learn: Iterate over subsets of the bad properties with sign (-1)^{|S|}; feasible when the number of properties is small (≤20) or symmetric.
Symmetric case: Σ_k (-1)^k C(m,k)·f(k) where f(k) counts objects violating k fixed properties.
Count numbers ≤n divisible by none of k primes with 2^k subsets of products (stop when the product exceeds n).
Upper bounds in stars and bars: subtract boxes that exceed their capacity via PIE.
Count gcd(b_i, b_{i-1}) constraints: factorize the ratio and use PIE over its distinct primes.
Grids with 'every row and column has a minimum': PIE over rows (and columns) that violate.

subtopics.name: Counting permutations: cycles, derangements & involutions
subtopics.summary: Counting permutations by structure: derangements D(n)=(n-1)(D(n-1)+D(n-2)), cycle decompositions, involutions, permutations with few fixed points, and permutations constrained by prefix maxima or by where values must go.
learn: Derangements: D(n)=n!Σ(-1)^k/k! or the recurrence (n-1)(D(n-1)+D(n-2)).
Permutation = disjoint cycles; the order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths.
Involutions (p(p(i))=i): I(n) = I(n-1) + (n-1)·I(n-2); each element is a fixed point or paired with another.
Place values from largest to smallest (or smallest to largest) and count free positions: products of (available slots) give the answer.
Prefix maxima / records: the maximum splits the permutation into independent left and right parts, combined with a binomial C(n-1, left size).
Count permutations with at most k misplaced elements: Σ C(n,i)·D(i).

subtopics.name: Stirling numbers, set partitions & sums of powers
subtopics.summary: Stirling numbers of the second kind S(n,k) count partitions of n labelled items into k non-empty groups; those of the first kind count permutations with k cycles. Their main contest use is rewriting x^k as a combination of falling factorials, which turns sums of k-th powers over subsets or random variables into sums of binomials.
learn: S(n,k) = S(n-1,k-1) + k·S(n-1,k); unsigned first kind c(n,k) = c(n-1,k-1) + (n-1)·c(n-1,k).
Surjections from n items onto k labelled boxes: k!·S(n,k) = Σ_i (-1)^i C(k,i)(k-i)^n (inclusion–exclusion), so one row S(n,·) is a single convolution.
x^k = Σ_j S(k,j)·x(x-1)...(x-j+1): turns Σ_{subsets} |S|^k into Σ_j S(k,j)·n!/(n-j)!·2^{n-j} in O(k^2).
E[X^k] for a binomial-like count X becomes Σ_j S(k,j)·j!·E[C(X,j)], and E[C(X,j)] is just a count of j-element subsets.
Bell numbers B(n) = Σ_k S(n,k) count all set partitions; Bell triangle or B(n+1) = Σ C(n,i)B(i).
Rook placements with exactly k attacking pairs, or n balls into k non-empty unlabelled boxes, are Stirling counts in disguise.

resources.title: Wikipedia: Stirling numbers of the second kind
Wikipedia: Stirling numbers of the first kind

subtopics.name: Catalan numbers, bracket sequences & reflection
subtopics.summary: C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1) counts balanced bracket sequences, binary trees, Dyck paths, triangulations. The reflection principle counts lattice paths that never cross a line, giving C(n+m,m) - C(n+m,m-1)-type answers.
learn: Catalan recurrence C_{n+1}=Σ C_i C_{n-i}; closed form C(2n,n)-C(2n,n+1).
Reflection: paths from (0,0) to (a,b) touching y=x+1 correspond bijectively to paths to a reflected endpoint.
Count bracket sequences with a fixed prefix: remaining opens/closes with the balance constraint via reflection.
Balanced sequences with forced matched intervals split into independent groups; multiply Catalan numbers per group.
Number of BSTs / binary trees with n nodes is C_n; with height constraints use DP on the Catalan recurrence.
Ballot problem / exceedance: the fraction of 'good' paths is often (a-b+1)/(a+1).

subtopics.name: Lattice paths, obstacles & the reflection principle
subtopics.summary: Monotone paths on a grid from (0,0) to (a,b) number C(a+b,a). With forbidden cells, sort them and subtract paths through the first forbidden cell (an O(k^2) DP over obstacles); with a forbidden line, reflect the endpoint. Recognise 'count walks/sequences of +1/-1 steps with a constraint on prefix sums'.
learn: Paths from (x1,y1) to (x2,y2) with right/up steps: C((x2-x1)+(y2-y1), x2-x1).
Obstacles: sort them, dp[i] = paths to obstacle i avoiding earlier obstacles = all paths − Σ_{j before i} dp[j]·paths(j→i); answer uses the target as the last 'obstacle'.
Reflection principle: paths that touch the line y = x + c are in bijection with paths to the endpoint reflected over that line.
Sequences of n (+1) and m (−1) with all prefix sums ≥ −k (or maximum prefix sum ≥ k) are counted by one reflection: C(n+m, m) − C(n+m, m−k−1) style formulas.
Expected / summed maximum prefix sum: Σ_k (number of sequences with max prefix ≥ k).
Probability that a queue never runs out of change (+10/−20 coins) is a ballot-type ratio of two binomials.

resources.title: CPH: Catalan numbers (paths in a grid)

problems.name: Natasha, Sasha and the Prefix Sums

subtopics.name: Counting trees: Cayley's formula & Prüfer codes
subtopics.summary: There are n^{n-2} labelled trees on n vertices (Cayley), proven via Prüfer sequences, where vertex v appears deg(v)-1 times. Generalisations count forests and ways to connect k components with sizes s_i: n^{k-2}∏s_i.
learn: Prüfer sequence: length n-2, bijection with labelled trees; degree of v = occurrences + 1.
Trees with prescribed degrees: (n-2)!/∏(d_i-1)!.
Connecting k components of sizes s_1..s_k into a tree: n^{k-2}·∏ s_i.
Forests of k rooted trees containing fixed roots: k·n^{n-k-1}.
Counting trees where a given path has length k: choose the path's inner vertices, then use the forest formula.
Matrix-tree theorem (Kirchhoff) counts spanning trees of any graph via a determinant.

problems.name: Sasha and Interesting Fact from Graph Theory

subtopics.name: Burnside's lemma & Pólya counting
subtopics.summary: Counts objects up to symmetry (rotations, reflections): the number of distinct objects equals the average number of configurations fixed by each symmetry. Classic use: necklaces and grid colourings up to rotation.
learn: Burnside: #orbits = (1/|G|) Σ_{g∈G} fix(g).
Rotation by k of an n-bead necklace has gcd(k,n) cycles, so fix = m^{gcd(k,n)}.
Group sums by d=gcd: Σ_{d|n} φ(n/d)·m^d / n.
Pólya: fixed colourings of a permutation with c cycles is m^c.
For grids under 90° rotations, count cycles of each rotation on cells.
Divide by |G| using a modular inverse.

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Burnside's lemma / Pólya enumeration theorem

subtopics.name: Generating functions
subtopics.summary: Encode a sequence a_n as the polynomial/power series Σ a_n x^n; products of generating functions combine independent choices, so counting questions become coefficient extraction, often finished with PIE or FFT.
learn: Ordinary GF of choosing 0..c items of a type: (1-x^{c+1})/(1-x); of unlimited items: 1/(1-x).
[x^n] (1-x)^{-k} = C(n+k-1, k-1); expand (1-x^{c+1}) products with PIE.
Exponential GFs (Σ a_n x^n/n!) handle labelled structures; products give binomial convolutions.
Products of many small polynomials are computed by divide & conquer with NTT.
Stirling numbers of the first kind are coefficients of x(x+1)...(x+n-1).
Catalan GF satisfies C(x)=1+xC(x)^2; solving needs polynomial sqrt/inverse.

resources.title: USACO Guide: More Complex Operations Using FFT

subtopics.name: Probability basics & probabilities mod p
subtopics.summary: Probability = favourable/total for uniform outcomes, multiplication for independent events, conditioning by cases. Many CF problems ask for the probability or expectation as P·Q^{-1} mod 998244353.
learn: Uniform outcomes: count favourable and total with combinatorics.
Independent events multiply; complementary event: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none).
Probability DP over steps: dp[state] = probability of reaching the state.
Print fractions mod p by multiplying with modular inverses; keep everything modular from the start.
Conditioning: P(A) = Σ P(A|B_i)P(B_i) over a partition of cases.
Double precision is fine when the output is a real number (CSES Dice Probability) — print enough digits.

subtopics.name: Expected value & linearity of expectation
subtopics.summary: E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] always, even for dependent variables. Write a complicated quantity as a sum of indicator variables and add their probabilities. The most frequent probability idea on Codeforces.
learn: Indicator trick: E[#good things] = Σ P(thing i is good).
Expected depth-like sums: in a random removal order, vertex v is chosen directly with probability 1/depth(v).
Expected number of pairs/inversions: sum over pairs of the probability the pair is 'good'.
E[X^2] = Σ_{i,j} E[X_i X_j] (expected square via pairs); for XOR, split into bit pairs.
Symmetry: in a random permutation each relative order of k fixed elements is equally likely.
Expected sum over all equally likely configurations = total sum / number of configurations (and vice versa).
Tail-sum formula for non-negative integers: E[X] = Σ_{k≥1} P(X ≥ k); E[max] is computed via P(max < k) = ∏ P(X_i < k).

problems.name: LuoTianyi and the Floating Islands (Easy Version)

subtopics.name: Expected-value DP & Markov chains
subtopics.summary: When a process repeats until a condition holds, write E[state] = cost + Σ p·E[next] and solve: by DP in topological order, by algebra when the state can return to itself (geometric distribution), or by Gaussian elimination for general Markov chains.
learn: Self-loops: E = 1 + pE + ... gives E = (1 + ...)/(1-p); expected trials until success with probability p is 1/p.
Process states backwards from the absorbing state (dp over 'remaining work').
Expected steps over a chain of states: linear equations E_i = a_i + b_i·E_0 solved by expressing everything in terms of one unknown.
Multiplicative/number-theoretic states: dp over divisors of the current gcd or prime exponents.
Coupon collector: expected draws to see all n types is n·(1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n); in general, sum the expected waiting times of each phase.
Markov chains: transition matrix powers give distributions after k steps; stationary distribution solves πP=π.

problems.name: Wish I Knew How to Sort

subtopics.name: Randomized algorithms
subtopics.summary: Use randomness to get algorithms that are correct with high probability: pick random elements that likely belong to the answer, random sampling in interactive problems, random hashing, and randomized checks. Requires a good RNG (mt19937).
learn: If the answer is supported by ≥ half the elements, a random element is in it with probability ≥ 1/2; repeat ~20-30 times.
Random candidate + full check (Monte Carlo / Las Vegas); estimate failure probability (1-p)^k.
Interactive search: random queries to find a large starting point before a deterministic walk.
Use mt19937 seeded with chrono time; never rand() (small range on Windows, hackable).
Majority/frequency queries on ranges by sampling random positions.
Randomly shuffle input to defeat adversarial worst cases (treaps, hashing, incremental algorithms).

resources.title: Don't use rand(): a guide to random number generators in C++

subtopics.name: Game analysis: parity, symmetry & mirroring
subtopics.summary: Two-player 'who wins with optimal play' problems where the answer follows from a parity count, a symmetric (mirroring) strategy, or a small invariant. Usually solved by playing small cases by hand and spotting the pattern.
learn: Brute-force tiny cases to find the pattern, then prove it with a strategy.
Mirroring: the second player copies the first player's move on the symmetric position.
Parity: if every move changes the state by a fixed amount, the winner depends on the parity of the total number of moves.
Strategy stealing: the first player can win if an extra free move cannot hurt.
Focus on terminal positions: who is forced to make the last move?
Tree games: the degree of the special vertex and parity of n often decide the winner.

subtopics.name: Winning/losing positions & game DP
subtopics.summary: A position is winning iff some move leads to a losing position; losing iff all moves lead to winning positions. Computing this by DP (or retrograde BFS on graphs with cycles) solves games with small state spaces and minimax score games.
learn: W/L rule: lose if no move exists (normal play); win iff exists a move to a losing state.
Compute in topological order (by remaining stones, positions sorted by value, interval length).
Score games (maximize own minus opponent's): dp[l][r] = max(a_l - dp[l+1][r], a_r - dp[l][r-1]).
Games on DAGs with two tokens: dp over (pos1, pos2, last letter, turn).
Graphs with cycles: retrograde analysis from terminal states with counters (draws remain undetermined).
Look for periodicity in W/L tables (1-2-k game: period 3, or period k+1 when k is divisible by 3).

subtopics.name: Nim & XOR-sum games
subtopics.summary: In Nim, the first player wins iff the XOR of pile sizes is non-zero. Many games are disguised Nim: staircase Nim (only odd-indexed steps matter), games where only the first non-trivial pile matters, and Nim with randomised piles.
learn: Nim: losing iff a1 ^ a2 ^ ... ^ an == 0; the winning move makes the XOR zero.
Misère Nim: same as Nim unless all piles are size 1 (then parity decides).
Staircase Nim: only piles on odd steps matter — it is Nim on those piles.
Sequential Nim (must take from the first non-empty pile): the player who first meets a pile >1 wins.
Removing the same amount from all piles: only the sorted distinct sizes/gaps matter.
XOR of ranges of consecutive integers has an O(1) formula (pattern by n mod 4).

subtopics.name: Sprague–Grundy theorem
subtopics.summary: Every impartial game position has a Grundy value = mex of the values of positions reachable in one move; a sum of independent games is losing iff the XOR of Grundy values is 0. Compute Grundy numbers by brute force, then find a pattern or periodicity.
learn: g(position) = mex{ g(next) }; g = 0 ⇔ losing.
Sum of games: XOR the Grundy values of independent components (piles, subtrees, rows).
Splitting moves (one pile into two) contribute g(a) ^ g(b) to the mex set.
Print the Grundy table for small inputs to find periodicity or a closed form (e.g. based on smallest prime factor).
State compression: Grundy values over bitmasks of used moves (Game of Stones) or of exponent sets.
Trees: Green Hackenbush value of a rooted tree is XOR over children of (child value + 1).

problems.name: Arpa and a game with Mojtaba

subtopics.name: Matrix exponentiation for linear recurrences
subtopics.summary: A linear recurrence f_n = Σ c_i f_{n-i} (+const) is a vector times a k×k transition matrix; raising the matrix to the n-th power with binary exponentiation computes f_n in O(k^3 log n) for n up to 10^18.
learn: Fibonacci: [[1,1],[1,0]]^n; extend the state vector with constants or prefix sums to handle +c or Σ terms.
DP with a fixed transition and huge length (counting strings/arrays of length 10^18 with local constraints) is matrix power.
Cost O(k^3 log n): keep k ≤ ~100; reduce state by symmetry or by digit residues.
Matrix products in a segment tree support range updates of recurrences (Fibonacci on ranges).
Exponents of multiplicative recurrences are reduced mod p-1 and powered as matrices.
Use unsigned long long accumulation and a single mod per entry to speed up the inner loop.
Fibonacci facts: gcd(F_m, F_n) = F_gcd(m,n); F_n mod k is periodic (Pisano period ≤ 6k); fast doubling computes F_n without matrices.
Advanced: Berlekamp–Massey finds the shortest linear recurrence from the first 2k terms; Kitamasa / polynomial mod computes the n-th term in O(k^2 log n).

subtopics.name: Walk counting, (min,+) products & matrices in segment trees
subtopics.summary: The (i,j) entry of A^k counts walks of length exactly k between i and j. Replacing (+,×) with (min,+) gives shortest walks with exactly k edges, and binary lifting on matrices answers 'smallest k with property' questions.
learn: Walk counting: (A^k)[i][j] = number of walks of length k from i to j.
Min-plus product: C[i][j] = min_k A[i][k] + B[k][j]; it is associative so fast exponentiation still works.
Shortest path with exactly k edges via min-plus power; with at most k by adding self-loops of cost 0.
Binary lifting over powers A^{2^j} to find the minimal length with a property (e.g. a positive cycle).
Boolean matrix powers with bitsets for reachability after k steps.
Edges unlocked over time: process time segments and multiply reachability matrices.
A DP whose transition is a small (min,+) or (max,+) matrix per position can be stored in a segment tree: each node keeps the product of its range, giving O(k^3 log n) range queries and point updates.
Aho–Corasick automaton states + (max,+) matrix power maximize a score over texts of length up to 10^14.

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Number of paths of fixed length / Shortest paths of fixed length

subtopics.name: Gaussian elimination (systems, rank, determinant)
subtopics.summary: Gauss–Jordan elimination solves n linear equations in O(n^3), computes rank, inverse and determinant, over reals or modulo a prime. Used for expected-value systems with cycles, linear systems mod p, and counting spanning trees.
learn: Pick a pivot (largest absolute value for doubles; any non-zero mod p), normalise the row, eliminate the column elsewhere.
Number of solutions: 0 if inconsistent, unique if rank=n, otherwise p^{n-rank} (mod p) or infinite.
Determinant = product of pivots with sign flips for row swaps.
Banded/tridiagonal systems (grid rows) solve in O(n) per row instead of O(n^3).
Expected values on graphs with cycles: one equation per state, then eliminate.
Over GF(2) use bitsets for O(n^3/64).
Recover a polynomial of degree k from k+1 sample values mod p by solving the Vandermonde system (or by Lagrange interpolation).

resources.title: cp-algorithms: Gauss method for solving system of linear equations
cp-algorithms: Calculating the determinant using Gauss
cp-algorithms: Finding the rank of a matrix

subtopics.name: XOR basis (linear basis over GF(2))
subtopics.summary: Treat numbers as vectors over GF(2); a basis of at most 60 vectors spans every XOR of a subset. Supports: max subset XOR, is x representable, number of distinct subset XORs (2^rank), and counting subsets with a given XOR (2^{n-rank}).
learn: Insert: for bits high→low, if the bit is set and basis[bit] exists XOR it out, else store as basis[bit].
Max XOR: greedily XOR basis vectors from the highest bit if it increases the value.
x is representable iff it reduces to 0; number of subsets with XOR x is 2^{n-rank} if representable.
Segments partition with no zero-XOR subset of segments: answer is the rank of prefix XORs.
Cycle space of a graph: XOR of a path between u,v can be changed by any cycle XOR; reduce with the basis of cycle XORs.
Square-free parity vectors (exponents mod 2) turn 'product is a perfect square' into a GF(2) rank problem.

resources.title: A Beautiful Technique for Some XOR Related Problems

problems.name: Mahmoud and Ehab and yet another xor task

subtopics.name: Prefix/range linear bases & bases on trees
subtopics.summary: Extensions of the XOR basis: keep the most recent index per pivot to answer 'max XOR in a[l..r]' offline or online, merge bases along tree paths (with LCA/divide & conquer), and count with basis-based combinatorics.
learn: Prefix basis keeping the largest index for each pivot answers max XOR on [l,r] using only vectors with index ≥ l.
Merging two bases costs O(log^2 C); combine with binary lifting, centroid or divide & conquer for tree paths.
Subtree/rerooting: bases of subtrees via Euler tour + prefix bases.
Graph cycle bases with dynamic components combine DSU and basis merging.
Counting subsets by popcount of XOR: enumerate the span when rank is small, otherwise use the orthogonal complement.
Rank changes at most log C times when adding vectors: amortised arguments.

resources.title: A Beautiful Technique for Some XOR Related Problems

subtopics.name: FFT & polynomial multiplication
subtopics.summary: The Fast Fourier Transform multiplies two polynomials of degree n in O(n log n). Any count of the form c[k] = Σ_{i+j=k} a[i]·b[j] (sums of pairs, matching with shifts, wildcard string matching) is a convolution.
learn: Convolution: c[k] = Σ_{i+j=k} a_i b_j; reverse one array to get correlations Σ a_i b_{i+k} (shift matching).
Use complex FFT with doubles for counts up to ~10^15 result precision; round results.
Wildcard/mismatch string matching: one convolution per alphabet letter, or Σ (a-b)^2 a b trick.
Count pairs (i,j) with a_i + a_j = s for all s using a frequency polynomial squared.
Repeated self-convolution (k items) via fast exponentiation of the polynomial with truncation.
Prefix-sum counts ('how many subarrays have exactly k elements less than x') become convolutions of count arrays.

resources.title: USACO Guide: Introduction to Fast Fourier Transform

subtopics.name: NTT & polynomial operations mod 998244353
subtopics.summary: The Number Theoretic Transform performs exact convolution modulo primes like 998244353 = 119·2^23+1 using a primitive root (3). Together with divide-and-conquer multiplication, polynomial inverse/log/exp, it solves most counting problems with generating functions.
learn: NTT replaces complex roots of unity with g^{(p-1)/n} mod p; works when n divides p-1.
Arbitrary modulus (10^9+7): three NTT primes + CRT, or split-FFT with doubles.
Product of many polynomials: divide & conquer (or a priority queue by degree) in O(n log^2 n).
Polynomial inverse by Newton iteration: B ← B(2 - AB) doubling the precision.
log/exp/power of power series allow 'k-fold product' and set-partition counts.
Watch sizes: pad to a power of two ≥ deg A + deg B + 1.

cp-algorithms: Operations on polynomials and series

subtopics.name: Walsh–Hadamard transform (XOR/AND/OR convolution)
subtopics.summary: Bitwise convolutions c[k] = Σ_{i⊕j=k} a_i b_j (XOR), and the AND/OR versions (zeta/Möbius transforms over subsets) run in O(n·2^n). They appear when combining masks, row/column flips and counting subsets by AND.
learn: FWHT for XOR: butterfly (u,v) → (u+v, u-v); inverse divides by 2^n.
OR convolution = subset-sum (zeta) transform, multiply pointwise, then Möbius transform.
AND convolution uses superset sums; counting subsets whose AND is 0 via PIE on superset counts.
Model 'flip some rows to minimise ones per column' as XOR convolution of column-mask counts with a cost function.
Combine with Fibonacci/linear transforms pointwise in the transformed domain.
Work modulo a prime with the inverse of 2^n.

resources.title: Fast Walsh Hadamard Transforms and its inner workings
USACO Guide: Sum over Subsets DP

subtopics.name: Polynomial interpolation & sums of powers
subtopics.summary: A polynomial of degree d is determined by d+1 values. When an answer is provably a polynomial in n of small degree (sums of k-th powers, DP values as a function of a huge parameter), compute it for d+1 small n and evaluate at the real n by Lagrange interpolation in O(d) or O(d^2).
learn: Lagrange: P(x) = Σ_i y_i ∏_{j≠i} (x - x_j)/(x_i - x_j); with x_i = 0..d use prefix/suffix products and factorials for O(d).
Σ_{i=1}^{n} i^k is a polynomial in n of degree k+1 (Faulhaber), so k+2 sample points suffice.
If dp[n][x] is a polynomial in x of degree ≤ n (e.g. salaries up to D with tree constraints), compute it for x = 0..n and interpolate at x = D.
Finite differences: the (d+1)-th difference of a degree-d polynomial is 0; shifting x by s changes the coefficient of x^{d-1} by d·s·a_d.
Recover all coefficients by Gaussian elimination on a Vandermonde system when d is tiny (≤ 10) and you can query values.
Everything is modulo a prime: precompute inverses of 1..d and handle x equal to a sample point separately.
